title: Back to the source
hook: ninth picture: rivers flow, flowers bloom, just as they are

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth picture: ox and self both forgotten, nothing but a circle. Your line: the empty circle. When did you drop the scorekeeper for a breath? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

After the empty circle, you might expect something grand: light, gold, a figure on a lotus. The ninth picture shows a river. A tree on its bank, a few flowers. Water moving past rocks. No herdsman, no ox, no circle. It looks like a page from any landscape painter's sketchbook. That's the surprise. After all that searching and letting go, the picture comes back to exactly the world we started in: the plain, ordinary world, seen clearly. Today: back to the source.
screen: `AFTER THE CIRCLE: A RIVER.` → `A TREE, A FEW FLOWERS.` → `THE ORDINARY WORLD, SEEN CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: First, it was clear from the start. The preface for this picture says, in paraphrase, that from the beginning things have been pure, with no dust on them. Nothing had to be built or added. The herdsman went through every stage only to see what was already the case. Second, the long way round. The verse has a line that's almost funny, in paraphrase: so many steps taken to get back to the root, it would have been better to be blind and deaf from the start. The point isn't that the journey was wasted. It's that the place he arrives is where he always stood. It is a little like coming home after a long trip and seeing your own street as if for the first time. Third, things as they are. The verse ends with the river flowing on, quietly, and the flowers simply red. The preface adds that the water is green and the mountains are blue. No symbolism. No lesson pinned to them. The river isn't a metaphor for time. The flowers aren't about beauty fading. They're a river and flowers, and that's enough. Fourth, watching without grabbing. The preface says he sits in stillness and watches things come together and come apart, without being caught by them. The empty circle didn't erase the world. It cleared away the reaching. And with the reaching gone, the world comes back, not as a problem to solve or a prize to win, but as it is. In this reading, the source isn't somewhere far away. It's a river on a Tuesday afternoon.
screen: `PURE FROM THE BEGINNING.` · `SO MANY STEPS TO GET BACK.` · `THE RIVER FLOWS, THE FLOWERS ARE RED.` · `WATCHING WITHOUT GRABBING.` · then, large: `JUST AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Find something living or moving to look at: a tree outside the window, a plant on a shelf, clouds, even the light on a wall. Sit and let your eyes rest on it. Don't name it, admire it or turn it into a lesson. Just let it be what it is: green, or moving, or still. When the mind starts commenting, come back to looking. A river flows. A flower is red. The bell holds the time.
Back to the source. The ninth oxherding picture: no herdsman, no ox, only a river and flowers, the world seen just as it is, as it was all along. Today's word.
Your line: just as it is. Today, look at one ordinary thing outdoors for ten slow breaths, and let it be exactly what it is. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Zen teachers point to the ninth oxherding picture to show that awakening, as this series describes it, returns to ordinary life rather than leaving it, and some teachers invite students to sit or walk outdoors and simply look.

fork.setup: after the empty circle, you're asked to paint the ninth picture. what does the series actually show?
options: a golden figure seated on a lotus.
a river and flowering tree, just as they are.
the ox returning with the herdsman.
fork.reveal: the ninth picture is a plain landscape. the series comes back to the ordinary world, seen clearly, with nothing added.

original.note: Chinese (fanben huanyuan): 'returning to the root, going back to the source', the name of the ninth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: back to the source means leaving the world for somewhere holy.
what it means: seeing the ordinary world just as it is, as it was all along.
what a scholar hears: the Chinese title pairs root and source, and the preface says things were pure from the beginning: the return is to where he always stood.

sources.ref: Ten Oxherding Pictures, picture 9: title, preface and verse
sources.work: Ten Oxherding Pictures, attributed to Kuoan Shiyuan (Kakuan)

notes: All oxherding material paraphrased. Check: preface (pure from the beginning, no dust; water green, mountains blue; sits in stillness watching things form and dissolve); verse (so many steps to return to the root, better blind and deaf from the start; the river flows on, the flowers are red).
Interpretive line 'the source is a river on a Tuesday afternoon' is the writer's; Keeper to confirm the reading of the ninth picture.
Original 返本還源; pronunciation approximates Mandarin fanben huanyuan.
Editor: myth item now states what the verse says rather than calling it a joke; howItsDone 'a common way' softened to 'some teachers'.
